name: Lena Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead press operator at a metal stamping plant on the edge of town. We stamp steel brackets and panels for washing machines and fridges, thousands a shift, on presses that come down with a bang you feel in your teeth. I set the dies, run the main line, check the first parts with a gauge and sign them off. My dad worked here thirty years and my grandfather before him, so I grew up hearing about these presses at the dinner table.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's it like working where your father worked?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Some of the old hands still call me Little Santos, and I let them, because it's affectionate. I'm proud of it, honestly. I'm getting married next spring to Mateo, he's a joiner, and we'll do the reception in the church hall like my parents did. I'm not one for phones and apps, I've never used any AI thing and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it anyway. I'd say it at Sunday lunch with the family, my uncle loves to talk about this. I don't post online, I don't really see the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my life goes ahead as planned. Wedding, a house near my parents, keep working the presses. That's all I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep saving, we've got a good amount put away for the house, and I'd keep training the two apprentices I've got. I'd let the office deal with any computer stuff, as long as it doesn't come down onto my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and relieved. Like when the doctor says it's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you train two apprentices. What do you teach them first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To respect the press before anything else. I make them stand and watch a full shift before they touch anything, like my dad made me. A press doesn't care how clever you are, it only cares whether your hands are out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anyone tried to get you to use AI tools at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young engineer, Felix, showed me some program that's supposed to predict when a die needs sharpening. I told him I can tell by the sound and the burr on the edge. He's a nice lad, but he's never been near a press when it's hot.

S0.say: I'd say good, I never trusted it anyway, mostly at Sunday lunch with my family. I don't post online because I don't see the point.
S0.think: For me it means my life goes ahead as planned, with the wedding, a house near my parents and the presses. That's all I want.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving for a house and keeps training her two apprentices. Leaves any computer systems to the office as long as they stay off her line.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like a doctor saying it's nothing.
S0.quote: A press doesn't care how clever you are, it only cares whether your hands are out of the way.
S0.fieldNote: Lena's identity is tied to family continuity at the plant and in the church. She takes pride in teaching apprentices the old way. She dismisses AI tools in favour of reading a die by sound, and a plateau simply confirms the life she has planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies should bring change in slowly and keep their people. If they want to modernise, fine, but train the workers and keep the apprenticeships going. I wouldn't want the government making a mess of it with schemes and handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about the apprentices more than me. I'm senior, they'd keep me to watch the machines, but they might stop taking young people on. My plant without apprentices would be like a church without children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep saving, maybe put the wedding budget down a little so we've more for the house. If they brought in new systems on my line, I'd learn them because I'd have to, but I'd ask for someone to show me in person, not a video. I'd talk to the plant manager about keeping the apprentice scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, mostly for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the plant manager, word for word?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mr Brandt, you started here as an apprentice, same as me. If you stop taking on young people, in fifteen years there'll be nobody left who knows what a press sounds like when it's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no government schemes. What if the plant couldn't afford to keep apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd rather the government helped the plant train people than paid people to sit at home. That's different, to me. Work is how you learn who you are.

S1.say: I'd say companies should bring change in slowly, keep their people and keep apprenticeships going. I wouldn't want the government making a mess of it with schemes and handouts.
S1.think: Privately I'd worry more for the apprentices than for myself, since a senior operator would be kept on. A plant without apprentices would be like a church without children.
S1.do: Keeps working and saving, trimming the wedding budget to put more towards the house. Learns new systems in person if required and lobbies the plant manager to keep the apprentice scheme.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly for the young apprentices.
S1.quote: If you stop taking on young people, in fifteen years there'll be nobody left who knows what a press sounds like when it's wrong.
S1.fieldNote: Lena's first concern is the line of succession at her plant rather than her own job. She separates help for training through employers, which she accepts, from paying people not to work, which she rejects. Her plea to the manager draws on their shared apprentice past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and somebody should have stopped it. I'd blame the tech billionaires who never set foot in a factory and don't care what happens to towns like ours. I'd say it after church, at work, to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened. I've only ever wanted this life, the same one my parents had. If the press I learned on is run by a robot in two years, I don't know what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding but make it small, family only, and put the rest into savings. We'd stop looking for a house and stay in the flat, maybe even move in with my parents for a while to save. I'd keep working until the last day they'd have me, and I'd lean on family and church to get through. I wouldn't know what to retrain for in two years, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd go quiet, and then he'd say we've had hard times before. He lived through the plant nearly closing in the nineties. But in the nineties they needed people to start the presses back up, and in this one they wouldn't need anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government support if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it. I'd try family first, and Mateo's work if he still had it. If there was truly nothing, I'd take it, but I'd feel ashamed, and I'd want it to be tied to some kind of work or training, not just money for nothing.

S2.say: I'd say it's madness and someone should have stopped it, blaming tech billionaires who never set foot in a factory. I'd say it after church, at work, to anyone.
S2.think: Privately I'd be frightened, because I only ever wanted the life my parents had. If a robot runs my press in two years, I don't know what I'm for.
S2.do: Keeps the wedding but makes it small and puts the rest into savings. Stops house hunting, may move in with her parents to save, works until the last day and leans on family and church.
S2.quote: But in the nineties they needed people to start the presses back up, and in this one they wouldn't need anyone.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI cuts straight through Lena's plan to repeat her parents' life. She contrasts the plant nearly closing in the nineties, when people were still needed, with a future where none are. She would accept government money only as a last resort and with shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for companies to do right by their people, so they'd better. I'd push for apprenticeships in new trades, not handouts. At church we'd probably organise something for families, like we did when the textile mill closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think five years is enough to get married and settled but not enough to feel safe. I'd be 32, maybe with a baby. And I'd still not know what to do instead of the presses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have the wedding as planned, and buy a small house, but cheaper than we'd hoped, so Mateo's pay could cover it. I'd keep working and keep saving hard. I'd wait a couple of years to see what the plant does before deciding anything, but if I had to, I'd go into something Mateo does, like working with wood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's there every time I think about a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does a baby make it worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because then it's not just my life. I'd be teaching my child to walk while a robot learns my job. I'd want to know there's something steady for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a couple of years. Is that a choice, or hard to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I'm slow with change, I know it, my mum says I'm the same as my dad. But I also don't want to jump into something new and find the robots got there first.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for companies to do right by their people, so they'd better. I'd push for apprenticeships in new trades rather than handouts, and our church would organise for families.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough to marry and settle but not to feel safe. I'd be 32, maybe with a baby, still not knowing what to do instead of the presses.
S3.do: Goes ahead with the wedding and buys a cheaper house that Mateo's pay could cover. Keeps working and saving hard, waits a couple of years to see what the plant does, and considers moving into woodwork alongside Mateo.
S3.feel: Anxious, especially whenever she thinks about having a baby.
S3.quote: I'd be teaching my child to walk while a robot learns my job.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Lena keep her life plans but pushes her to scale them down. A future child sharpens her worry. She admits her waiting is partly temperament inherited from her father and partly fear of retraining into something robots reach first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time enough to keep our towns together, if business and families take the lead. I'd want companies running apprenticeships for whatever comes next. I'd say it at church and at work, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd have a normal start to married life, maybe two children. But by 2036 they'd be small and growing up into a world where nobody needs a press operator. That bothers me more than my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years, nothing changes, keep working, keep training apprentices, buy the house. I'd keep saving for the children. Around year five I'd maybe do a course in something steady, perhaps woodwork with Mateo, or something in the church school, but I'd take my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but slowly. Like a long drive with a storm on the horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Faith, and how to work hard. And something with their hands, even if robots can do it, because it teaches you patience. I'd teach them to make things even if nobody needs them made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of ten years that gives you hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If people take it seriously, families and churches could organise. The village came together when the mill closed, and nobody needed the government to tell them how.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time enough to keep our towns together if business and families take the lead. I'd want companies running apprenticeships for whatever comes next, said at church and work, not online.
S4.think: Privately ten years gives me a normal start to married life, maybe with two children. By 2036 they'd be growing up where nobody needs a press operator, which bothers me more than my own job.
S4.do: Keeps working, training apprentices and buys the house in the first few years while saving for children. Around year five, may take a course in something steady such as woodwork with Mateo or a role at the church school.
S4.feel: Anxious but slowly, like a long drive with a storm on the horizon.
S4.quote: I'd teach them to make things even if nobody needs them made.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Lena's worry moves from her own job to the children she expects to have. She places her hope in families and church rather than government, citing the mill closure. She still plans to change slowly and on her own terms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the one that would take the life I planned and throw it out before I even started it. I always thought I'd stand at the same press as my dad until I was his age. What would help is the companies keeping their workers on through the change, and apprenticeships for new trades, so people can earn while they learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it does to towns. A plant like ours isn't just jobs, it's the football team, the church fair, the people you see at the bakery. If that goes, it's not something money fixes.

headlineQuote: I always thought I'd stand at the same press as my dad until I was his age.
portrait: Lena Santos, 27, is lead press operator at the metal stamping plant where her father and grandfather worked, and trains two apprentices the old way. She is engaged to Mateo, a joiner, plans a church wedding and a house near her parents, and avoids AI tools entirely. A plateau leaves her relieved, and steady disruption worries her mostly for the apprentices. Fast AGI alarms her and leads her to shrink the wedding, put off the house and lean on family and church. With five or ten years she keeps her plans but scales them down, and her worry moves to the children she hopes to have.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would throw out the life she planned before she even started it.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping their workers on through the change and offering apprenticeships in new trades so people can earn while they learn.
